title: The passive back-rank defence
summary: Against a knight's or rook's pawn, waiting on the first rank is enough. Against the others it is not.
part.wait.title: Waiting on the first rank
part.wait.summary: Against a knight's pawn, king in front of the pawn and rook on the first rank are enough.
part.corner.title: The corner and the bishop's pawn
part.corner.summary: Black's only trick, and why the same defence loses against a bishop's pawn.
part.home.title: Back home and recap
part.home.summary: When the rook must return to the first rank, the rook's pawn, and the rules for your games.
step.intro: There is not always time to set up the Philidor defence. Here the black king is already on the third rank and the knight's pawn is on the third. What is left is the most modest defence there is: the king in front of the pawn and the rook on the first rank, shielding the king from checks. It looks like little, and against this pawn it is enough. Black has no way in.
step.wait: Wait. The rook goes back and forth along the first rank. There is only one moment that needs thought: when the black rook checks on g2.
step.wait.hint: Rc1, Rb1 and, on the check on g2, the king goes to the corner: Kh1. Then it returns to g1.
step.wait.done: Black tried everything there was. Your rook never even left the first rank.
step.corner: This is Black's only trick, and it is worth a close look. The rook has checked on g2. The king has two squares, and only one draws: the corner. On h1 the black rook has to leave, and the king returns to g1. On f1 the black king enters on h2, gets in front of the pawn, and the game is lost.
step.lucena: That is what happened here: the king went to f1 and the black king entered on h2. The pawn will advance protected, your king is cut off from the queening square, and the black rook builds the bridge: it is the Lucena position, which you know from the other side. King to the corner, never outwards.
step.room: Why does the defence work against the knight's pawn? Because the black rook would need to go round to the other side of your king to threaten mate on the first rank, and on that side there is only the h-file. There is no room. Remember this idea, because it explains the rest of the lesson.
step.bishop: Now the same thing with a bishop's pawn. The black rook checked on g2, the king went to f1, and the rook switched to h2: it threatens mate on h1. If the king returns to g1, the pawn advances with check and the rook mates or wins yours. One more file for the black rook, and the passive defence loses. Against a bishop's pawn or a central pawn with the attacking king already on the third rank, the back rank does not work.
step.free: So what do you do against a bishop's or central pawn? Do not reach that position. Here the black king has not yet entered the third rank: it is one move short. This is the time to drop the passivity. The rook goes to the far end and checks from behind, as in Philidor.
step.active: Leave the first rank while there is time. Rook to the far end, and checks.
step.active.hint: Rb8. When the king enters on g3, Rg8+; then Rf8+.
step.active.done: The black king cannot get in and protect the pawn at the same time. One move later, with the king already on g3, it would be lost.
step.behind: The opposite also exists. With a knight's pawn it is the active defence from behind that fails: your king can only run to the long side, and Black cuts it off. Here the rook is at the far end and the pawn is about to advance. It has to return to the first rank, and the way is via the a-file.
step.home: Bring the rook home: along the eighth rank to the a-file, and from there to the first.
step.home.done: Back on the first rank, with the king in front of the pawn: it is the position from the start of the lesson. Staying behind the pawn with the rook, on g8, would lose.
step.rookPawn: With a rook's pawn it is simpler still. The king in the corner, the rook on the first rank, and there is no trick at all: the black rook has no file whatsoever on the other side. A draw without thinking.
step.recap: What to take away. One: against a knight's or rook's pawn, king in front of the pawn and rook on the first rank draw. Two: on the rook check, the king goes to the corner. Three: against a bishop's or central pawn the back rank loses if the attacking king reaches the third rank; get out earlier, with the rook to the third rank or to the far end.
step.t_knight: A knight's pawn on the third rank, the black king beside it, and no time left for the Philidor defence. You defend with White. How could Black make progress, and what stops them?
step.t_knight.hint1: Think about where the black rook would need to go to threaten mate on the first rank, and how much room it has for that.
step.t_trick: The black rook has checked on g2. Your king has two squares. Which one draws, and what happens on the other?
step.t_trick.hint1: After your move, see whether the black king can get in front of the pawn.
step.finish: Now against the machine: wait with the rook on the first rank and, when the check comes, go to the corner.
ex.e10: White to move and draw. A bishop's pawn on the fourth rank, the black king beside it, and your rook on the first rank. Can you wait, as against the knight's pawn?
ex.e10.hint: Count how many moves the black king needs to enter the third rank, and remember what happens against a bishop's pawn once it does.
ex.e10.solution: Rc3, and after f3, Rc8; when the king goes to g3, Rg8+. It is the Philidor defence, set up from the first rank. Waiting with the rook on the first rank would lose to the king's advance.
ex.e11: White to move and draw. A rook's pawn already on the seventh, and the black rook threatens to come down to the first rank. Where does the king go?
ex.e11.hint: With a rook's pawn the corner is the safest square there is. And if your king ends up with no moves, think about what that could be worth.
ex.e11.solution: Kh1, in front of the pawn. Kf1? loses at once: h1=Q is mate. After Ra3, besides waiting on the first rank (Rc1, Rd1, Re1 or Rf1), there is a pretty resource: Rb3+! If the black rook takes, it is stalemate, because your king has no square; if the black king steps out of check, Rxa3 wins the rook. Position from Hemanthsankar's study on Lichess.
ex.e15: White to move and draw. A knight's pawn, the black king beside it on the third rank. Stay on the first rank or go behind the pawn?
ex.e15.hint: Against a knight's pawn, what happens if the black rook checks along the first rank and your rook is not there?
ex.e15.solution: Stay: Rb1 (or Rd1, Re1, Rf1; Kh1 and Rc3+ also hold). Against a knight's pawn the first rank draws. Going to the far end, Rc8?, loses: Ra1+ and the king, with no h2 and no g2, has to go to f2, the long side; the black king enters on h2 and the pawn gets through.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Your rook is on the short side, on h8. Coming back to the first rank along the h-file looks natural. Is it?
ex.e12.hint: See who gets the h1 square if the rook comes down the h-file. Before going home, push the black king out of the way.
ex.e12.solution: Rf8+! and, after Kg3, Rf1: the rook returns to the first rank via the f-file, not the h-file. Rh1? takes the corner away from the king: Rg2+ forces Kf1 and the black king gets in. On the check on g2, the corner, Kh1, as in the lesson. Our own position, checked against the tablebase.
ex.e14: White to move and draw. A knight's pawn, but your king is not in front of it yet, and the rook is far from the first rank. Where do you start?
ex.e14.hint: The rook can wait. The king cannot: which square does it need to take away from the black king?
ex.e14.solution: Kf2!, which takes g3 away from the black king; Kf1? allows Kg3 and the black king arrives first. After Rd2+, Kg1! (the pawn's corner). If Kh3, Re3+ or Re1 hold; after g3, Re1, and it is the passive defence from the lesson. King first, rook second. Study by IsaacWiebeSupreme on Lichess.
ex.e16: White to move and draw. A central pawn on the seventh, and your king can blockade it. After that, every rook move counts.
ex.e16.hint: The black rook wants to come down to the first rank with check. Your rook has to be on the first rank, but not on just any square of it: think about a rook trade and about the pawn.
ex.e16.solution: Ke1, blockading the pawn; Kd2? loses to Kf2. Then the rook dances along the first rank: Rc3 Rb1, Ra3 Rc1, Rb3 Ra1. It never stands on the black rook's file (Rxa1+ trades rooks and the pawn queens) nor on d1 (the pawn takes). On any other square of the first rank, the black rook's check is met by capturing it. Our own position, checked against the tablebase.
key.knight: The passive defence against a knight's pawn, as shown on Wikipedia (quoting Emms), with colours reversed: a draw.
key.trick: The only trick: on the rook check the king goes to the corner. The other way loses.
key.bishop: With a bishop's pawn the same defence loses: the attacking rook has one more file to go round. From Wikipedia, with colours reversed.
key.seventh: Pawn on the seventh and king beside it: the rook defends from the first rank with only moves. From Wikipedia (quoting Emms), with colours reversed.
history: The passive defence has no illustrious name and no date: it is what remains when Philidor's was not set up in time. The manuals treat it as a rule of thumb. Grandmaster Hovhannes Gabuzyan sums it up like this: against pawns on the c, d, e and f files you need to know the Philidor defence; against those on the a, b, g and h files the back rank is enough. Wikipedia, drawing on Averbakh and Kopaev, adds the detail that saves half a point: if the attacking king has not yet reached the sixth rank, there is still time to leave the passive defence with the rook, to the third rank or to the far end, against any pawn.
practice: Against the machine: a knight's pawn, your rook on the first rank and the king in front of the pawn. Wait, and on the check go to the corner. The goal is to draw.
